# PRODUCTS OF UNITARIES AS CONTINUOUS EVOLUTIONS AT FINITE PRECISION

Abstract. I present a short approach to discretizing continuous unitary evolution. It gives a correspondence in both directions between continuous unitary evolutions and products of unitaries in finite dimensions, and I use it to reduce discrete adiabatic theorems to continuous ones. At fine steps, holding truncated samples of a regulated Hamiltonian on a suitable finite partition gives an approximating product. Conversely, rounding the clock identifies a product of _T_ unit-step samples with a continuous evolution, up to two half-step phases. I bound its operator-norm distance from the original evolution by _O_(1_/T_) through cancellation within each time step. This assumes bounded first and second derivatives, bounded spectral width, and eigenvalue differences bounded away from nonzero multiples of \(2\pi\), uniformly in _T_. For a unitary walk with these derivative bounds, a fixed common free spectral arc supplies a Hermitian logarithm path satisfying the comparison hypotheses. Continuous simulation guarantees then transfer to the phase-corrected product, and continuous adiabatic bounds to the product itself, with an explicit additive _O_(1_/T_) error and each adiabatic theorem’s hypotheses retained. For positive definite quantum linear systems of condition number \(\kappa\), this comparison and continuous adiabatic theory give a rescaled quobitized walk with \(O(\kappa/\delta)\) steps for leakage \(\delta\), matching the scaling previously obtained through a discrete adiabatic theorem. These products need no discrete adiabatic theorem.

### 1. Discretizing unitary evolution

Simulating continuous-time evolution within the quantum circuit model typically requires applying a finite product of unitaries or, equivalently, generating unitaries from a piecewise-constant Hamiltonian. Thus, a continuous evolution generated by _H(t_) is approximated by a finite product whenever a piecewise-constant Hamiltonian family _G(t_) generates approximately the same evolution. Holding matrix entries at finite precision can already define _G_.

I use this observation to carry theorems between continuous evolutions and products of unitaries. In one direction, truncating a Hamiltonian’s entries builds a product, and conversely, under the hypotheses below, rounding time compares unit-step samples with the path’s own continuous evolution. Adding the comparison error to a continuous adiabatic bound then gives a discrete result that retains the continuous theorem’s hypotheses.

We begin with bit truncation because it makes the connection concrete. Fix an energy unit and truncate each entry’s real and imaginary parts toward zero at the _k_th binary place, obtaining _H_<sup>(_k_)</sup>. When this is constant on finitely many time intervals, its induced product _W_ has one exponential per interval, with generator and duration determined by the truncation (Definition 2.1), and we compare it with the evolution _U(T_) generated by _H_.

This gives a finite product when the real and imaginary parts of the entries are piecewise monotone, but even a smooth entry can cross one truncation level infinitely often. Holding truncated midpoint samples on a chosen partition instead approximates every regulated family, one with one-sided limits at every time (Definition 2.3). Finite total variation \(\ell\), measured in operator norm, lets us control variation within intervals by placing checkpoints at equally spaced variation levels (Definition 3.5 and Lemma 3.6). In these fine-step constructions, we choose precision and refine the partition for accuracy.

<tbc>For the fine-step comparison and its adiabatic consequences, we use two standard facts. First, if _U_ and _V_ are the evolutions of _H_ and _G_ starting at the identity, differentiation gives<tbc>

\(\frac{d}{dt}(U^\dagger V)=iU^\dagger(H-G)V.\)

<tbc>Integrating gives, in the operator norm used throughout, the Duhamel estimate (Lemma 2.4, \[4\])

\(\|U(T)-V(T)\|\le\int_0^T\|H(t)-G(t)\|dt\le Tsup_t\|H(t)-G(t)\|.\)

Our second tool is the Davis-Kahan \(sin\Theta\) theorem \[10\]. A continuous adiabatic theorem bounds the leakage between spectral subspaces of _H_(0) and _H(T_), the largest norm, over unit vectors in the initial subspace, of the evolved vector’s component outside the final subspace (Definition 2.6). If these endpoint subspaces are instead taken from the truncated matrices, Davis-Kahan bounds their change by the Hamiltonian error divided by the spectral gap (Theorem 2.7), and this change adds to the leakage bound.

## 1.1. Main results.

We summarize the comparisons informally, calling a matrix \(\sigma\)-sparse when each row has at most \(\sigma\) nonzero entries (Definition 2.2).

**"Theorem" A.** _Let H be a regulated,_ \(\sigma\)_-sparse Hermitian family on_ \[0_,T_\]_, with evolution U starting at the identity. If its entrywise k-bit truncation H_<sup>(_k_)</sup> _is piecewise constant, the induced product W, one exponential per constant piece, satisfies_

\(\|W-U(T)\|\le\sqrt{2}\sigma 2^{-k}T.\)

Otherwise, we use truncated midpoint samples (Lemma 3.8).

**"Theorem" B.** _For a regulated,_ \(\sigma\)_-sparse Hermitian family H on_ \[0_,T_\] _with total variation_ \(0<\ell<\infty\)_, holding truncated midpoint samples between equal-variation checkpoints gives a product within_ \(\varepsilon\) _of U(T), with_ \(O(T\ell/\varepsilon)\) _factors and_ \(O(log_2(\sigma T/\varepsilon))\) _bits as_ \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\).

To apply this comparison, traverse a fixed path over time _T_, preserving its variation \(\ell\). If a continuous theorem bounds leakage between its endpoint subspaces by _C/T_, with _C\>_0 depending on the path, choosing _T_ proportional to \(C/\delta\) and evolution error proportional to \(\delta\) gives leakage \(O(\delta)\). The standard fine-step count is \(O(\ell C/\delta^2)\), with about \(2log_2(1/\delta)\) bits for fixed \(\sigma\), _C_, and \(\ell\) (Corollary 3.15).

Bit precision is one choice of levels for holding values fixed, and the layer-cake construction, which allows other levels and also applies to time, starts from the identity \[20\]

\(x=\int_{(0,\infty)}\mathbf{1}_{\{\lambda\le x\}}d\lambda(x\ge 0).\)

Replacing \(d\lambda\) by positive point masses, finitely many in each bounded range, gives a step function _F(x_). Applied to magnitudes of entries’ real and imaginary parts, with signs restored, its discrepancy |_F(x_)-_x_| controls Hamiltonian error. Equal masses 2<sup>-_k_</sup> at positive multiples of 2<sup>-_k_</sup> recover bit truncation (Section 5).

Holding the clock, rather than the entries, at finite precision gives the converse comparison, in which a product of unit-step samples approximates the path’s own continuous evolution, up to two half-step phases and _O_(1_/T_) under the hypotheses below. Take a Hermitian family _H_ on \[0,1\], with _U_ evolving under _H(t/T_) for \(0\le t\le T\), and for integer \(T\ge 1\) put

\(W_T=e^{-iH((T-1)/T)}\cdots e^{-iH(1/T)}e^{-iH(0)}.\)

Unit masses at the positive half-integers give the rounded clock \(q(t)=\lfloor t+1/2\rfloor\), so _H(q(t)/T_) holds each sample on a centered unit interval, with half intervals at 0 and _T_. Its evolution is exactly \(e^{-iH(1)/2}W_Te^{iH(0)/2}\) at time _T_.

Direct Duhamel comparison integrates an _O_(1_/T_) Hamiltonian error over time _T_ and gives only an _O_(1) bound, so instead a Hermitian correction, the frame, cancels first-order changes within each centered interval and takes equal values at its ends. The second-order remainder and neighboring-frame differences contribute _O_(1_/T_<sup>2</sup>) per interval, and the ends contribute _O_(1_/T_) (Lemma 6.2 and Theorem 5.5). Separation of the samples’ eigenvalue differences from nonzero multiples of \(2\pi\) bounds the frame (Lemma 2.9 and Remark 2.10).

**"Theorem" C.** _For integer_ \(T\ge 1\)_, let H be a twice continuously differentiable Hermitian family on_ \[0,1\] _with_ \(\|H'\|\le L\) _and_ \(\|H''\|\le 2\nu\)_, U its evolution under H(t/T_) _starting at the identity, and_ \(W_T=e^{-iH((T-1)/T)}\cdots e^{-iH(1/T)}e^{-iH(0)}\)_. Suppose each interior sample H(j/T),_ 0_\<j\<T, has spectrum in an interval of length at most_ \(\bar{w}\)_, and its nonzero eigenvalue differences lie at distance at least_ \(\gamma>0\) _from every nonzero multiple of_ \(2\pi\)_, with L,_ \(\nu\), \(\gamma\)_, and_ \(\bar{w}\) _independent of T. Then_

\(\big\|e^{-iH(1)/2}W_Te^{iH(0)/2}-U(T)\big\|=O_{\gamma,\bar{w}}\big((L+L^2+\nu)/T\big).\)

Thus, operator-norm bounds comparing _U(T_) with a target also hold for the phase-corrected product, adding _O_(1_/T_) error (Theorem 6.4). Since the half-step phases preserve the endpoint spectral subspaces, any continuous adiabatic bound on endpoint leakage then transfers to _W<sub>T</sub>_ under these comparison hypotheses, retaining the continuous theorem’s hypotheses (Theorem 6.5). A continuous _C/T_ bound therefore gives \(O(1/\delta)\) unit steps for target leakage \(\delta\) (Corollary 6.7).

For quantum linear systems, which ask for the state \(A^{-1}b/\|A^{-1}b\|\), take _A_ positive definite of condition number \(\kappa\), with \(\|A\|=\|b\|=1\). An and Lin’s path \[2\] (Definition 6.8), with speed proportional to the 3/2 power of its gap lower bound, satisfies the comparison hypotheses with error \(O(\kappa/T)\). Their gap bound and the continuous Jansen–Ruskai–Seiler theorem \[16\] give leakage \(O(\kappa/T)\), so \(O(\kappa/\delta)\) factors suffice (Corollary 6.9).

A walk is an ordered sequence of unitaries (Definition 6.10). For samples of a _C_<sup>2</sup> unitary family whose spectra avoid a common open arc, a Hermitian logarithm cut inside that arc gives an _O_(1_/T_) evolution comparison, up to half-step phases (Theorem 6.11), and adiabatic transfer retains the continuous theorem’s hypotheses on this logarithm path. Appendix A constructs a rescaled qubitized walk, a product of two reflections encoding the Hamiltonian \[21\], for quantum linear systems with such an arc. Given preparation of _b_, it recovers Costa et al.’s \(O(\kappa/\delta)\) query count \[8\], with constant success probability signaled by a measurement and state-vector error at most \(\delta\), up to global phase.

### 1.2. Prior work and outline.

Earlier discrete adiabatic theorems take unit steps as given and impose conditions on their variation and eigenphase (eigenvalue-argument) gaps \[27, 8\]. Yi and Crossson apply continuous adiabatic theory to logarithms of Trotter steps assuming negligible discretization error \[31\], while Theorem 6.11 bounds the product’s operator-norm distance from the logarithm’s evolution by _O_(1_/T_), up to the half-step phases, under the stated regularity and free-arc hypotheses. For the sampled exponentials _e_<sup>-_iH(j/T_)</sup>, _O_(1_/T_) leakage is known for nondegenerate spectra \[30\], under multistep-gap hypotheses \[1\], and asymptotically for a ground state \[23\], whereas Theorem 6.4 compares evolutions in operator norm without requiring gaps between spectral bands, allowing levels to cross.

Section 2 prepares the comparison tools, and Section 3 develops bit truncation, fine-step comparison, and adiabatic transfer. Section 4 counts truncation-level crossings and compares with time sampling, while Section 5 extends truncation to other levels and proves the bound assembling piecewise comparisons for unit steps. Section 6 applies the construction to time, proves unit-step transfer, and treats quantum linear systems and walks. Section 7 discusses applications, open questions, and implementation, and Appendix A gives the walk circuit and query count.

## 2. Preliminaries

In this section, we define the evolutions and induced products used throughout the paper. Duhamel and Davis–Kahan prepare the fine-step comparison and its adiabatic transfer, while the frame operator prepares the unit-step comparison. Throughout, \(d\ge 1\), _T\>_0, and every Hamiltonian family takes Hermitian values. For \(H,G:[0,T]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}\), the unitary evolutions _U,V_ solve

(2.1) \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c }
i\dot{U}(t)=H(t)U(t), \\
U(0)=1,
\end{array}\right.\left\{\begin{array}{ c }
i\dot{V}(t)=G(t)V(t), \\
V(0)=1.
\end{array}\right.\)

**Definition 2.1.** A family _G_ is _piecewise constant_ if there are times \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=T\) and matrices _G_<sub>0</sub>_,...,G_<sub>_n_-1</sub> with _G(t_)=_G<sub>j</sub>_ on each _piece_ (_t<sub>j</sub>,t_<sub>_j_+1</sub>). The _t<sub>j</sub>_ are its _piece endpoints_. Its _induced product_ is

(2.2) \(W=e^{-i(t_n-t_{n-1})G_{n-1}}\cdots e^{-i(t_2-t_1)G_1}e^{-i(t_1-t_0)G_0},\)

with one unitary per piece, applied in the order of time.

**Definition 2.2.** A matrix is \(\sigma\)_-sparse_, for a positive integer \(\sigma\), if each row has at most \(\sigma\) nonzero entries.

Truncation changes at most \(\sigma\) entries per row, so entrywise precision 2<sup>-_k_</sup> gives operator-norm error \(O(\sigma 2^{-k})\) (Lemma 3.3). The regularity we ask of _H_ at fine steps is the following.

**Definition 2.3.** A map _H_ from \[0_,T_\] to the \(d\times d\) matrices is _regulated_ if it has a limit from the right at every \(t\in[0,T)\) and a limit from the left at every \(t\in(0,T]\).

Lipschitz families are regulated, but regulated families may also jump, and their one-sided limits permit the uniform piecewise-constant approximations \[11, (7.6.1)\] needed for the fine-step comparison.

For a regulated family, we read (2.1) in the following sense: _U_ is continuous and unitary-valued, _U_(0)=1, and \(i\dot{U}(t)=H(t)U(t)\) for all but countably many _t_. The same applies to _V_ , and Proposition 2.5 proves existence and uniqueness in this sense. For piecewise-constant _G_, the evolution is _V(t_)=_e_<sup>-_i(t-t<sub>j</sub>)G<sub>j</sub>_</sup>_V(t<sub>j</sub>_) on \[_t<sub>j</sub>,t_<sub>_j_+1</sub>\], so _V(T_)=_W_ in (2.2), whatever the values of _G_ at the piece endpoints _t<sub>j</sub>_.

## 2.1. Comparing two evolutions.

The Duhamel estimate \[4\] allows countably many exceptional times at which the evolutions need not be differentiable.

**Lemma 2.4.** _Let_ \(H,G:[a,b]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}\)_, let_ \(S\subset[a,b]\) _be countable, and let_ \(U,V:[a,b]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}\) _be continuous and unitary-valued, with U(a_)=_V(a), such that_ \(i\dot{U}(t)=H(t)U(t)\) _and_ \(i\dot{V}(t)=G(t)V(t)\) _for every_ \(t\in[a,b]\backslash S\)_. If_ \(t\mapsto\|H(t)-G(t)\|\) _is integrable, then_<tbc>

(2.3) \(\|U(b)-V(b)\|\le\int_a^b\|H(t)-G(t)\|dt.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For \(t\in[a,b]\backslash S\), the product rule and the two evolution equations give \(\frac{d}{dt}(U^\dagger V)=iU^\dagger(H-G)V\) , whose norm is \(\|H-G\|\) by unitarity. The fundamental theorem of calculus for a continuous function with integrable derivative outside a countable set (see \[11, (8.7.1)-(8.7.2)\] for regulated derivatives) gives

\(U(b)^\dagger V(b)-1=i\int_a^bU(t)^\dagger\big(H(t)-G(t)\big)V(t)dt,\)

since _U(a_)<sup>†</sup>_V(a_)=1. Taking norms, using the integral triangle inequality and unitary invariance of the norm, gives (2.3). □

For a uniform bound \(\|H(t)-G(t)\|\le\eta\), integration gives \(\|U(b)-V(b)\|\le\eta(b-a)\), so \(\|U(T)-W\|\le\eta T\) for piecewise-constant _G_. Duhamel also constructs the evolution of a regulated family.

**Proposition 2.5.** _Every regulated family_ \(H:[0,T]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}\) _is bounded and has at most countably many discontinuities, hence a set of discontinuities of measure zero. It has a unique continuous unitary evolution U, with U_(0)=1_, satisfying_

\(U(t)=1-i\int_0^tH(s)U(s)ds.\)

_At every continuity point of H,_ \(i\dot{U}(t)=H(t)U(t)\)_, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. In particular, U satisfies the equation at all but countably many times._

_Proof._ Choose piecewise-constant Hermitian \(H_n\rightarrow H\) uniformly, each equal to _H_ at its piece endpoints \[11, (7.6.1)\]. Uniform convergence makes _H_ bounded and continuous outside the countable union of partition points. Their unitary evolutions _U<sub>n</sub>_ satisfy \(sup_t\|U_n(t)-U_m(t)\|\le Tsup_t\|H_n(t)-H_m(t)\|\) by Lemma 2.4, so they converge uniformly to a continuous unitary _U_ with _U_(0)=1. Passing to the limit in \(U_n(t)=1-i\int_0^tH_n(s)U_n(s)ds\) gives the integral equation, since the integrands converge uniformly. At continuity points of _H_, the integrand _H(s)U(s_) is continuous, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the stated derivatives. Finally, Lemma 2.4 with identical generators gives uniqueness. □

## 2.2. Spectral projectors.

For adiabatic transfer, Davis-Kahan lets us replace endpoint subspaces by those of truncated matrices, with error proportional to truncation error over the gap (Lemma 3.9).

**Definition 2.6.** For a Hermitian matrix _H_ and a compact interval _I_, the _spectral projector P<sub>I</sub>(H_) projects orthogonally onto the span of the eigenvectors of _H_ with eigenvalues in _I_. For \(\Gamma>0\), _H_ has a _gap_ \(\Gamma\) _around I_ if every eigenvalue of _H_ outside _I_ lies at distance at least \(\Gamma\) from _I_, and _I_<sup>+</sup> is _I_ extended by \(\Gamma/2\) at each end. The _leakage_ of a matrix _X_ from a projector _P_ to a projector _Q_ is \(\|(1-Q)XP\|\).

For a unitary _X_, the squared leakage bounds the probability of finding \(X\psi\) outside the range of _Q_ for every unit vector \(\psi\) in the range of _P_.

**Theorem 2.7** (Davis-Kahan, \(sin\Theta\left[10\right]\))**.** _Let_ \(H,G\in\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}\) _be Hermitian, let I,J be compact intervals, and suppose every eigenvalue of G outside J lies at distance at least_ \(\Gamma>0\) _from I. Then_<tbc>

\(\left\|(1-P_J(G))P_I(H)\right\|\le\frac{\left\|(1-P_J(G))(H-G)P_I(H)\right\|}{\Gamma}\le\frac{\|H-G\|}{\Gamma}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _m,c_ be the midpoint and half-width of _I_, and put _P=P<sub>I</sub>(H_) and _Q_=1-_P<sub>J</sub>(G_). The spectral hypotheses give \(\|(H-m1)P\|\le c\) and \(\|(G-m1)Qv\|\ge(c+\Gamma)\|Qv\|\). Since _P_ commutes with _H_ and _Q_ with _G_, for every unit vector _v_,

\((c+\Gamma)\|QPv\|\le\|(G-m1)QPv\|=\|QP(H-m1)Pv+Q(G-H)Pv\|\le c\|QP\|+\|Q(G-H)P\|.\)

Taking the supremum over _v_ and subtracting \(c\|QP\|\) gives the first inequality, and projector contraction gives the second. □

See \[5, Theorem VII.3.1, (VII.30)\]. Kostrykin, Makarov, and Motovilov \[18\] already compare a spectral projector with that of the perturbed operator for the half-gap neighborhood of an isolated spectral part, as we do in Lemma 3.9, treating general spectral parts under a smallness condition on the perturbation. Yu, Wang, and Samworth \[32\] give a variant for eigenvectors indexed by eigenvalue order, with an eigengap assumed for one matrix only.

## 2.3. The derivative of the exponential.

Returning from unit-step products to continuous evolution uses the frame operator for comparison under separation (Section 6), and the inverse averaging operator for a walk’s logarithm (Section 6.3). Both come from differentiating a step, which averages conjugated changes in its generator over the whole step \[6, Lemma 2\],

(2.4) \(\left.\frac{d}{ds}e^{-i(H+sE)}\right|_{s=0}=-ie^{-iH}\int_0^1e^{i\tau H}Ee^{-i\tau H}d\tau.\)

**Definition 2.8.** For a matrix _H_, the _averaging operator_ is<tbc>

\(\Phi_H(E)=\int_0^1e^{i\tau H}Ee^{-i\tau H}d\tau,\)

<tbc>and the commutator map is _a<sub>H</sub>(E_)=_i(HE-EH_). The _spectral width_ of _H_ is the length of the smallest interval containing its eigenvalues. Write _B<sub>n</sub>_ for the Bernoulli numbers, with \(B_1=-\frac{1}{2}\). For \(0\le w<2\pi\) and \(x\notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}\backslash\{0\}\), put

\(\mathcal{B}(w)=\sum_{n\ge 0}\frac{\left|B_n\right|}{n!}w^n,\mathcal{N}(x)=\frac{1-\frac{x}{2}cot\frac{x}{2}}{x^2},\mathcal{N}(0)=\frac{1}{12}.\)

For _H_ with no eigenvalue difference in \(2\pi\mathbb{Z}\backslash\{0\}\), the _frame operator_ \(\Theta_H\) multiplies the (_p,q_) entry of a matrix, written in an eigenbasis of _H_ with eigenvalues \(\lambda_p\), by \(\mathcal{N}(\lambda_p-\lambda_q)\). For \(\gamma>0\), a Hermitian matrix is \(\gamma\)_-separated_ if each of its eigenvalue differences _x_ satisfies _x_=0 or \(|x-2\pi n|\ge\gamma\) for every nonzero integer _n_.

Integrating \(e^{i\tau H}Ee^{-i\tau H}=e^{\tau a_H}(E)\) over \[0,1\] gives \(\Phi_H=(e^{a_H}-1)/a_H\), interpreted as a power series. The spectral width is at most _w_ exactly when _H_ is within _w/_2 of a real multiple of the identity, and then \(\|a_H\|\le w\). Euler’s formula \(\left|B_{2m}\right|/(2m)!=2\zeta(2m)/(2\pi)^{2m}\) for \(m\ge 1\), with \(\zeta(2m)<2\), gives \(\left|B_n\right|/n!\le 4(2\pi)^{-n}\), so B converges for \(w<2\pi\) and bounds the inverse averaging operator (Lemma 2.9). The even function N is regular at 0 and has poles at nonzero multiples of \(2\pi\) (Remark 2.10).

In Section 6, a Hermitian frame absorbs the generator’s first-order change around the midpoint sample _h_ of each interior unit interval and takes the same value at both ends, so neighboring frames nearly cancel. That common value is \(\Theta_h(D)\), for the generator’s slope _D_, and it solves (2.5), which fixes its entries at nonzero eigenvalue differences through the multiplier N. The entries at zero differences are unconstrained, and choosing \(\mathcal{N}(0)=lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\mathcal{N}(x)=1/12\) keeps \(\Theta_h\) continuous in _h_ across eigenvalue coincidences. **Lemma 2.9.** _Let_ \(h,\tilde{h}\) _be Hermitian._ (1) _Suppose that_ \(\gamma>0\) _and_ \(h,\tilde{h}\) _are_ \(\gamma\)_-separated of spectral width at most_ \(\bar{w}\)_. The frame operator_ \(\Theta_h\) _preserves Hermitian matrices and, for every matrix D, solves_ \(e^{ih}\Theta_h(D)e^{-ih}-\Theta_h(D)=\int_0^1\big(\tau-\frac{1}{2}\big)e^{i\tau h}De^{-i\tau h}d\tau.\) \(\text{(2.5)}\) _Moreover,_ \(\|\Theta_h\|\le N_\gamma,\|\Theta_h-\Theta_\tilde{h}\|\le N'_\gamma\|h-\tilde{h}\|,\) _with dimension-independent constants depending only on_ \(\gamma\) _and_ \(\bar{w}\). (2) _If_ \(h,\tilde{h}\) _have spectral width at most_ \(w<2\pi\)_, they are_ \(\gamma'\)_-separated for every_ \(0<\gamma'\le 2\pi-w\)_. In this case, the frame-operator bounds hold with_ N(_w_) _and_ \(2\mathcal{N}'(w)\) _in place of_ \(N_\gamma\) _and_ \(N'_\gamma\). (3) _If_ \(h,\tilde{h}\) _have spectral width at most_ \(w<2\pi\)_, the inverse averaging operator used for walks is_ \(\Phi_h^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge 0}\frac{B_n}{n!}a_h^n.\) _It preserves Hermitian matrices, with_ \(\|\Phi_h^{-1}\|\le\mathcal{B}(w),\|\Phi_h^{-1}-\Phi_\tilde{h}^{-1}\|\le 2\mathcal{B}'(w)\|h-\tilde{h}\|.\) _Proof._ In an eigenbasis of _h_, let \(x=\lambda_p-\lambda_q\). Comparing the multipliers of _Dpq_ reduces (2.5) to \((e^{ix}-1)\mathcal{N}(x)=\int_0^1\big(\tau-\frac{1}{2}\big)e^{i\tau x}d\tau.\) Both sides vanish at _x_=0. For \(x\notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}\), \((e^{ix}-1)\mathcal{N}(x)=\frac{e^{ix}-1}{x^2}+\frac{e^{ix}+1}{2ix}\text{since}\mathrm{cot}\frac{x}{2}=\frac{i(e^{ix}+1)}{e^{ix}-1},\)
\(=\int_0^1\big(\tau-\frac{1}{2}\big)e^{i\tau x}d\tau\text{integrating by parts.}\) Since N is real and even, the frame preserves Hermitian matrices entrywise. The eigenvalue differences allowed by \(\gamma\)-separation and width at most \(\bar{w}\) form a compact set avoiding the poles. Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff \(\chi=1\) there, supported away from the poles, and let _g_ be the Fourier transform of the smooth extension \(\chi\mathcal{N}\). Fourier inversion gives \(\Theta_h(D)=\int_\mathbb{R}g(s)e^{2\pi ish}De^{-2\pi ish}ds\), so unitary invariance gives \(N_\gamma=\|g\|_1\). Duhamel bounds \(\|e^{2\pi ish}-e^{2\pi is\tilde{h}}\|\) by \(2\pi|s|\|h-\tilde{h}\|\) on each side of _D_, giving \(N'_\gamma=4\pi\int_\mathbb{R}|sg(s)|ds\), finite because _g_ decays faster than any power. If \(|x|\le w<2\pi\) and \(n\neq 0\), then \(|x-2\pi n|\ge 2\pi|n|-|x|\ge 2\pi-w\). For (2)-(3), \(\|a_h\|\le w<2\pi\), and since a scalar shift of _h_ preserves _ah_ and gives \(\|h\|\le w/2<\pi\), the inverse formula follows from \[6, Lemma 3\] applied to _ih_. For the explicit bounds of (2), since \(|x|\le w<2\pi\), the convergent series \(\sum_{n\ge 0}B_{n+2}a_h^n/(n+2)!\) mul tiplies entry (_p,q_) by (_z/(ez_-1)-1+_z/_2)_/z_2 at _z=ix_, which is N(_x_) because _z/(ez_-1)+_z/_2=(_z/_2)coth(_z/_2), (_ix/_2)coth(_ix/_2)=(_x/_2)cot(_x/_2), and _z_2=-_x_2. So this series is \(\Theta_h\), and \(\mathcal{N}(x)=\sum_{m\ge 0}(-1)^mB_{2m+2}x^{2m}/(2m+2)!\), since odd Bernoulli numbers past _B_1 vanish. Since \(\|a_h^n\|\le w^n\) and (-1)_mB_2_m_+2=|_B_2_m_+2|, the absolute coefficient sums bound the operator norms by B(_w_) and N(_w_). Telescoping powers with \(\|i[h-\tilde{h},E]\|\le 2\|h-\tilde{h}\|\|E\|\) gives \(\|a_h^n-a_\tilde{h}^n\|\le nw^{n-1}\|a_h-a_\tilde{h}\|\le 2nw^{n-1}\|h-\tilde{h}\|\) for \(n\ge 1\). Termwise differentiation of the majorants then gives the Lipschitz bounds. Both series preserve Hermitian matrices, since their coefficients are real and _ah_ preserves Hermiticity. □

## 3. Fine steps

In this section, we use Duhamel to match products at finite precision to continuous evolution, then Davis-Kahan to transfer leakage bounds. A coordinate _h_ of _H_ is a real function of _t_, and 2_k_\[_h(t_)\]_k_ is its _grid level_. A family is _piecewise monotone_ if its coordinates are monotone on each interval of a finite partition. **Proposition 4.2.** _Let_ \(k\ge 0\) _be an integer and_ \(0=\xi_0<\xi_1<\cdots<\xi_N=T\) _be times such that every coordinate of H is monotone on each interval_ \([\xi_r,\xi_{r+1}]\)_. ## 5. Layer-cake truncation and comparison

In this section, we extend bit truncation to levels that may better suit a problem, replacing \(d\lambda\) in the layer-cake identity \[20\]

\(x=\int_{(0,\infty)}\mathbf{1}_{\{\lambda\le x\}}d\lambda(x\ge 0)\)

with any level measure. We bound the Hamiltonian error, count pieces, and recover the fine-step comparison of Lemma 3.8, before proving the assembly bound (Theorem 5.5) used at unit steps in Section 6.

**Definition 5.1** (Level measure)**.** A _level measure_ \(\mu\) is the Stieltjes measure of a nondecreasing, right- continuous function _F_, zero on \((-\infty,0]\) and taking finitely many values on every \[0_,R_\]. Thus, \(F(x)=\mu((0,x])\) for \(x\ge 0\). Set

\([x]_\mu=\int_{(0,\infty)}\mathbf{1}_{\{\lambda\le x\}}d\mu(\lambda)=F(x)(x\ge 0),[-x]_\mu=-[x]_\mu.\)

Applying this entrywise to real and imaginary parts defines \(H^{(\mu)}\). The _discrepancy_ on \[0_,R_\] is \(D_R(\mu)=sup_{0\le x\le R}|x-F(x)|\). The _crossing number_ \(cr_\mu(x,y)\) is one less than the number of distinct values \([z]_\mu\) for \(min(x,y)\le z\le max(x,y)\). It counts the levels that a coordinate moving monotonically from _x_ to _y_ crosses, so it bounds how many times its truncation changes. For a map _q_ on \[0_,T_\], a _layer_ is a pre-image _q_<sup>-1</sup>({_v_}).

Discussion At finite precision, products of unitaries and continuous evolutions are the same object, whichever we start from. Holding the entries at finite precision turns a continuous evolution into a product within \(\sqrt{2}\sigma 2^{-k}T\) of it (Lemmas 3.4 and 3.8). Holding the clock at finite precision turns a product of unit steps from a smooth path with separated samples back into that path’s own evolution, up to the half-step phases and _O_(1_/T_) (Theorem 6.4). Theorems therefore transfer between the two settings, and a theorist can derive a discrete result from its continuous counterpart instead of proving it again. The quantum linear systems problem shows what this buys, since there the continuous theorem and the comparison together recover the \(O(\kappa/\delta)\) count that was previously obtained through a discrete adiabatic theorem (Corollaries A.2 and 6.9). Because the comparisons concern evolutions rather than adiabatic transport, I expect them to help wherever a time-dependent evolution is simulated. Existing methods choose their discretization from the Hamiltonian in different ways. Wiebe, Berry, Høyer, and Sanders choose step lengths from the local size of the derivatives of _H_ \[29\]. Berry, Childs, Su, Wang, and Wiebe rescale time by \(\|H(t)\|\), so that costs scale with \(\int\|H(t)\|dt\) rather than \(Tmax_t\|H(t)\|\) \[4\]. In Low and Wiebe’s interaction-picture algorithm, the average of \(\|\dot{H}\|\) controls the number of discretization points and enters the cost logarithmically \[22\]. Poulin, Qarry, Somma, and Verstraete avoid smoothness assumptions altogether by sampling at random times \[25\]. Holding entries at finite precision needs neither derivatives nor random times, so I expect its equal-variation checkpoints to complement these methods. Each factor it produces is time-independent, and qubitization \[21\] can implement it. On analog hardware, a device whose finite-resolution controls truncate the entries of _H_ in a fixed basis implements _H_(_k_)(_t_), so Lemma 3.4 applies to it, and so does Theorem 3.11 whenever _H_(_k_) is piecewise constant, as it is for piecewise-monotone _H_ (Proposition 4.2). The correspondence is first order, and that leaves its main open questions, since some continuous theorems give much more than _O_(1_/T_). For gapped Gevrey families whose derivatives all vanish at the two ends, the continuous leakage has bounds of the form exp(-_cTa_), with _c\>_0 and 0_\k_, which, for a fixed piecewise-monotone path rescaled to \[0_,T_\], is like \(T/\varepsilon\)

and outgrows every power of _T_ for these bounds. Can polynomially many factors retain the same leakage decay? At unit steps, the correction 1-_iY_ of Lemma 6.2 cancels only the linear drift, so the question becomes which additional corrections or endpoint hypotheses would let faster-decaying bounds transfer.

A second question concerns growth in _T_. The time-discretization error of a sampled adiabatic product need not grow with _T_ [30, 19, 1, 23], and I would like the same for entry truncation. At fixed precision _k_, when is its contribution to adiabatic leakage bounded independently of _T_? Theorem 6.4 rounds the clock but keeps exact samples, so it does not answer this. Derivative bounds on _H_ alone need not answer it either, because truncating a linearly moving coordinate produces a sawtooth error that could resonate with the spectral gap. A third question is whether the unit-step comparison extends to contracting evolutions [3], which Cunningham and Roland obtain by applying unitaries at Poisson-distributed times and averaging over realizations [9]. The obstacle is that the correction 1-_iY_ of Lemma 6.2 need not be a contraction.

Finally, some costs lie outside this paper. Direct truncation needs the times at which entries cross truncation levels, which an oracle for _H(t_) does not return. Lemma 3.8(2) avoids this by computing checkpoints from the variation \(\ell(t)\), or from any computable nondecreasing \(\varphi\) with \(\|H(t)-H(s)\|\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)\) for \(s\le t\). For adiabatic applications, preparing a state in the initial spectral subspace and testing for the final one are further tasks.
